newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-Chancellor Schmidt says jobless major EU issue.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Chancellor Schmidt says jobless major EU issue.

text.p: Former German Chancellor Helmut Schmidt warned on Monday that persistently high unemployment rates, not the preparations for Europe's currency union, were Germany's and Europe's biggest problems.
"It is not the Maastricht Treaty that stands to threaten the stability of domestic policy but rather unemployment," Schmidt told a banking forum.

But Schmidt predicted that Europe's planned currency union would be launched on time on January 1 1999, largely because European politicians are determined to see the currency come and as its benefits outweighed its potential drawbacks.

Schmift however said there was a 15 percent chance that the currency union would not go ahead as planned. If that occured, Germany might see its position threatened as other nations could join together to form an alternative block.
At the same time Schmidt highlighted Germany's fear of giving up the deutschemark but portrayed this as the typical German fear of all things unknown.

"The Germans are prone to hysteria against everything that is new," he said, citing mistrust of innovations in biotechnology, plans for a futuristic magnetic levitation train and new technology in general.
"For Germans everything should stay as it always has been," Schmidt said.
Schmidt recommended that Germans should take tough action on several issues, including agreeing to keep wages steady for a number of years.

Austerity measures would be easier to accept if business leaders offered an example by keeping their own wages steady and not accepting bonus packages such as shares in their own companies, a move often viewed as a way of boosting shareholder value, Schmidt said.
